beats.text: On the evening of May 21, 1796, the President of the United States sat down to dinner in Philadelphia.

overlays.hook: She ran away from George Washington.

beats.text: While George and Martha Washington ate, a young woman they enslaved walked out of the house.
She never came back. And for the rest of his life, the most powerful man in America tried to get her back.
He wrote letters. He asked his Treasury Department for help. He sent his own nephew to seize her.

visual.caption: Runaway ad for Oney Judge, May 1796

beats.text: Her name was Ona Judge. This is the story of the woman who escaped George Washington, and was never caught.
Ona Judge was born around 1773 at Mount Vernon, the Washingtons' plantation in Virginia.
Her mother, Betty, was enslaved. Her father, Andrew Judge, was a white English tailor working as an indentured servant.
Under Virginia law, a child followed the status of the mother. So Ona was born enslaved.
Betty belonged to Martha Washington's first husband's estate. People like her were called dower slaves.
That mattered. Legally, George Washington could not free them, even if he wanted to. They were held for Martha's heirs.
When Ona was about ten, she was brought into the mansion house.
She became Martha Washington's personal maid. She dressed her, served her, and went wherever she went.
In 1789, George Washington became the first President of the United States.
The government sat in New York, and the Washingtons brought enslaved people from Mount Vernon to run the household. Ona, about sixteen, was one of them.
The next year, the capital moved to Philadelphia. Ona was one of nine enslaved people taken to the President's House.
But Pennsylvania had a law. Under its Gradual Abolition Act, an enslaved person brought into the state who stayed for six months in a row could claim freedom.
So the Washingtons kept the clock from running out. They rotated the people they enslaved out of Pennsylvania, back to Virginia or across the state line, before the six months were up.
In 1791, Martha Washington took Ona to Trenton, New Jersey, for two days. Just long enough to reset the clock.
Philadelphia had a large and growing free Black community. Ona saw, every day, people like her living free.
In the spring of 1796, Washington was in his last year as President. Soon the family would go home to Virginia for good.
Then Ona learned something. Martha Washington planned to give her away, to her granddaughter, Eliza Custis Law.

visual.caption: Eliza Custis Law, Martha Washington's granddaughter

beats.text: She would be handed over like property, to a new owner, and taken back to Virginia.
Decades later, she remembered what she thought.

visual.quote: I knew that if I went back to Virginia, I should never get my liberty.

beats.text: So while the Washingtons packed to go to Virginia, she packed too. She did not know where she was going.
She had friends among the free Black people of Philadelphia. Quietly, her belongings were carried out of the house ahead of time.
On May 21, 1796, while the President and the First Lady sat at dinner, Ona Judge walked out the door.
Her friends got her onto a ship commanded by Captain John Bowles, bound north for Portsmouth, New Hampshire.
Three days after she vanished, an advertisement appeared in the Philadelphia Gazette.
Absconded from the household of the President of the United States, it read. It described her freckles, her very black eyes, and her bushy hair.
The reward was ten dollars, to anyone who brought her back.
But by then, she was already at sea.
In Portsmouth, Ona Judge found work, and began a new life among the town's free Black residents.
Then, one day that summer, someone recognized her on the street.
It was Elizabeth Langdon, the daughter of a United States senator, John Langdon. She had visited the Washingtons, and she knew exactly who Ona was.
Word reached the President.
On September 1, 1796, Washington wrote to his Secretary of the Treasury, Oliver Wolcott, asking for help to have her seized and sent back by ship.

visual.caption: Oliver Wolcott Jr., Secretary of the Treasury

beats.text: Wolcott passed the job to the customs collector in Portsmouth, Joseph Whipple.
Whipple found Ona and asked her to board a ship back to Virginia.
She said no. But she made an offer. She would go back, if the Washingtons promised to free her when they died.
Whipple would not force her onto a ship. He passed her offer to the President.
Washington refused. To enter into such a compromise, he wrote, was totally inadmissible.

visual.quote: To enter into such a compromise... is totally inadmissible.

beats.text: Ona Judge stayed. In early 1797, she married a free Black sailor named Jack Staines.
That March, Washington left the presidency and went home to Mount Vernon. He had not forgotten her.
In August 1799, he wrote to his nephew, Burwell Bassett Junior, who was going to New Hampshire on business.
His request: seize Ona, and her baby, and bring them back to Virginia.
Bassett found her, and tried to talk her into coming back. She refused.
So he planned to take her by force. And he made a mistake. He told Senator Langdon.
Langdon sent her a secret warning. That night, Ona Judge took her baby daughter and fled to the town of Greenland, a few miles away.
Bassett went home empty-handed.
On December 14, 1799, George Washington died at Mount Vernon.

visual.caption: The tomb of George Washington, Mount Vernon

beats.text: He had chased her for more than three years. He never got her back.
In his will, Washington freed the people he himself enslaved, after Martha's death.

visual.caption: The Washington Family, by Edward Savage

beats.text: But Ona was not his. She was a dower slave, held for the Custis heirs. Nothing in that will could free her, or her children.
Martha Washington died in 1802. In law, Ona Judge was still a fugitive slave.
A federal law, the Fugitive Slave Act of 1793, signed by George Washington himself, allowed people who escaped to be captured and returned.
For the rest of her life, she lived with that.
Freedom was hard. Ona and Jack had three children. Then, in 1803, Jack Staines died.
She could not support her family alone. She moved in with the Jacks family in Greenland.
Her daughters were bound out as indentured servants. Both died before her.
In old age, she was poor, and relied on gifts from her community.
But she had chosen her own faith, and her own church. And she had chosen her own life.
In 1845, an abolitionist newspaper in New Hampshire, the Granite Freeman, published an interview with her. A second one followed in The Liberator.
She was in her seventies. She told how she had walked out on the President of the United States.
She was asked if she was sorry she had ever left the Washingtons.
Her answer: No, I am free, and have, I trust, been made a child of God by the means.

visual.quote: No, I am free, and have, I trust, been made a child of God by the means.

beats.text: Ona Judge died in Greenland, New Hampshire, on February 25, 1848. She was about seventy-five.
She had outlived George Washington by almost fifty years. By law, she was still a fugitive.
Today, at the site of the President's House in Philadelphia, her story is told where it happened.
She was enslaved by the first President of the United States.
She walked out of his house while he ate dinner, and he spent the rest of his life trying to get her back.
He never did.
That was Ona Judge. Subscribe for more.
